goals.text: Predict which option greedy, ε-greedy and UCB pick next, and explain why greedy can lock onto a worse option while ε-greedy and UCB keep exploring, each in its own way.

segments.title: The problem: three restaurants, hidden averages
Exploit only, its lock-in, and ε-greedy

facts.text: You repeatedly choose one of several options, called arms, for example which of three restaurants to eat at every night for 300 days.
facts.ask: So what do I actually choose between each time, and how many times do I get to choose?

facts.text: Each arm gives a random reward from its own distribution, and these distributions and their averages are hidden at the start.
facts.ask: Do I know in advance how good each option is, or what I'll get when I pick it?

facts.text: The goal is to collect as much total reward as possible over all the rounds, not only to find out which arm is best.

misconception.says: So this is basically full reinforcement learning, where what I pick changes the situation I'm in next?
misconception.truth: In a bandit, choices don't change the situation: there are no states. Only the information you gather carries over.

probes.open: So what exactly is the problem we're solving here? What do I get to choose each time?
probes.why: Why can't I just figure out which arm is best before I start?
probes.whatIf: What if there were 100 restaurants instead of 3, would it still be the same kind of problem?
probes.compute: If restaurant 1 averages 10 happiness and I eat there all 300 days, how much happiness do I expect in total?

facts.text: An arm's value is estimated by the average (mean) of the rewards it has given so far.
facts.ask: How do I put a number on how good an option seems so far?

facts.text: The estimate changes every time the arm is tried, and estimates from only a few tries can be far from the true average.
facts.ask: Can I trust that number after only one or two tries?

probes.open: How do I even keep track of which arm seems better so far?
probes.why: Why is the average the right thing to look at, and not just the last reward?
probes.whatIf: What if the best restaurant gave me a really bad meal on my first visit, just by bad luck?
probes.compute: An arm gave rewards 2, 9 and 4. What's my estimate for it?

facts.text: Greedy (exploit only) always picks the arm with the best average so far, for example after trying each restaurant once.
facts.ask: Once I have those numbers, what's the simplest rule for choosing?

facts.text: Greedy never tries an arm on purpose to learn more, so arms that looked bad early are never tried again.
facts.ask: With that rule, would I ever go back to an option that looked bad early on?

misconception.says: Isn't always picking the one that looks best just the smartest thing to do?
misconception.truth: Early estimates are noisy. Greedy can lock onto a worse arm because it never collects the data that would correct the estimate.

probes.open: Once I have some averages, what's the most obvious way to choose?
probes.why: Why would I ever pull an arm that looks worse?
probes.whatIf: What if two arms are tied on their average, what does this rule do?
probes.compute: My averages so far are 7, 8 and 5. Which arm does greedy pick next, and when does it pick the 5 one again?

facts.text: Because greedy only goes back to the current best, one unlucky early reward from the truly best arm can hide it for the rest of the game.
facts.ask: What could go wrong with greedy if the best option happens to give a bad result the first time?

facts.text: Example: if restaurant 1 (mean 10) happens to give 7 on day one and restaurant 2 (mean 8) gives 8, exploit only eats at restaurant 2 for the remaining 297 days.
facts.ask: Can you show me with the restaurants how that could actually happen?

facts.text: Being stuck costs the gap between the two arms' averages on every remaining round.

probes.open: Could greedy ever get it wrong and never notice?
probes.why: Why wouldn't greedy just try the other arm again later?
probes.whatIf: What if the best arm had paid really well on its first try instead?
probes.compute: If restaurant 2 averages 8 and restaurant 1 averages 10, and I'm stuck at restaurant 2 for 297 days, how much happiness do I miss out on?

facts.text: ε-greedy picks a random arm with a small probability ε (for example 10%) and otherwise picks the arm with the best average so far.
facts.ask: Is there a way to mostly pick the best one but still try the others now and then? How would that work?

facts.text: Its random picks ignore the estimates, so it spends as many of them on arms already known to be bad as on arms it knows little about.
facts.ask: When it does try something else, how does it decide which one to try?

facts.text: With 3 arms and ε = 0.1, the arm that currently looks best is picked with probability 0.9 + 0.1/3 ≈ 0.93.

misconception.says: So when it picks randomly, it goes for the arms it's least sure about, right?
misconception.truth: No: ε-greedy picks uniformly at random, regardless of how uncertain each arm is.

probes.open: Is there a way to keep using my best guess but still try the others sometimes?
probes.why: Why pick a random arm instead of the one I know least about?
probes.whatIf: What if ε were 0, or 1? What would happen then?
probes.compute: With 3 arms and ε = 0.1, how likely is it that I pick the arm that currently looks best?

facts.text: Exploration means trying arms to learn about them; exploitation means picking the best arm you know of to collect reward.
facts.ask: Is there a name for trying options to learn about them, versus sticking with my favourite?

facts.text: Too little exploration risks locking onto a worse arm; too much exploration wastes rounds on arms you already know are worse.
facts.ask: What goes wrong if I try new things too rarely, or too often?

facts.text: How much exploration pays off depends on how far apart and how noisy the arms are, and on how many rounds are left.

misconception.says: So exploring more is always the safe choice?
misconception.truth: Every exploratory pull of a worse arm costs reward; with a constant ε that cost keeps growing.

probes.open: It feels like I'm always torn between trying new places and going back to my favourite. Is that a real problem?
probes.why: Why not just try everything a lot at the start and then decide?
probes.whatIf: What if I only had 5 days in town instead of 300?
probes.compute: If I explore on 10% of 300 days by picking one of 3 restaurants at random, about how many days do I spend at the worst one because of exploring?

facts.text: UCB1 picks the arm with the highest score: its average plus a bonus √(2 ln t / n), where t is the current round (day) and n is the number of times that arm was tried.
facts.ask: Is there a smarter way to score each option, instead of picking at random? How is the score made?

facts.text: The average is the exploitation part and the bonus is the exploration part: arms tried only a few times get the benefit of the doubt.
facts.ask: Why would that score favour options I've hardly tried?

facts.text: UCB1 is deterministic: with the same history it always picks the same arm.

misconception.says: So UCB sometimes just picks an arm at random to try it out?
misconception.truth: No. UCB1 is deterministic; it explores by adding a bonus to arms it has tried few times.

probes.open: Is there a smarter way to pick which place to try than rolling a die?
probes.why: Why add something to the average instead of just using the average?
probes.whatIf: What if two arms have the same average but one was tried 100 times and the other once?
probes.compute: After 10 rounds, arm A was tried 5 times with average 0.6 and arm B 3 times with average 0.7. Which does UCB1 pick? (ln 10 ≈ 2.3)

facts.text: Each time an arm is tried its n goes up, so its bonus shrinks and it becomes less likely to be picked just to learn more about it.
facts.ask: What happens to an option's bonus each time I try it?

facts.text: The ln t on top grows slowly with every round, so an arm that has been ignored for a long time eventually gets tried again.
facts.ask: Could an option I haven't tried for ages ever get picked again?

probes.open: What happens to an arm's chances right after I finally try it again?
probes.why: Why does trying an arm make it less likely to be chosen the next day?
probes.whatIf: What if I never pick an arm for a very long time, does it get forgotten?
probes.compute: An arm tried 4 times at a round where ln t = 2 has bonus √(2·2/4) = 1. What's its bonus after 16 tries at the same round?

facts.text: An average based on one visit is much less reliable than one based on a hundred visits.
facts.ask: How much should I trust an average from one visit compared with one from a hundred?

facts.text: So comparing averages alone ignores how many samples each is based on: 2.9 from 1 visit could really be higher than 3 from 100 visits.
facts.ask: If two options have about the same average, does it matter how many times I tried each?

probes.open: If two places have almost the same average, is there anything else I should look at before choosing?
probes.why: Why is one visit not enough to trust an average?
probes.whatIf: What if one place averaged 2.9 from a single visit and the other 3 from 100 visits?
probes.compute: One restaurant: 1 visit, average 2.9. Another: 100 visits, average 3. Which has the higher average, and which estimate could be further off?

contradictions.question: Wait, if I eat at restaurant 2 tonight, does that change how good restaurant 2 will be tomorrow?
But what if the best place just had an off night the one time I went there?
When it picks something other than the favourite, does it look at which place it knows least about, or does it just roll a die?
If I explore on every single day, how much happiness do I give up compared with always going to the best place?
If I eat at the best restaurant every night but get a few bad meals, does that count as regret too?
If I gave UCB the exact same history twice, could it pick different restaurants?
What if a restaurant gets a new chef halfway through the year, does my old average still tell the truth?

goalChecks.question: Over 100 rounds I pulled the 0.8 arm 60 times and the 0.5 arm 40 times. How much did I lose compared with always pulling the best one? And how much would greedy lose if it got stuck on the 0.5 arm for all 100 rounds?

Two arms have the same average, but one was tried 1,000 times and the other 3 times. Which one would ε-greedy pick when it isn't picking randomly, which one would UCB1 pick, and which of the two rules loses less over a very long time?
goalChecks.expects: ε-greedy sees a tie and ignores the counts; UCB1 picks the arm tried 3 times because its bonus is larger. Over a long time UCB1 loses less: its bonus shrinks so exploration fades and regret grows logarithmically, while a constant ε keeps exploring and regret grows linearly.

goalChecks.question: A news site wants to choose one of 4 headlines for each visitor. How would you set it up as a bandit, and would you use ε-greedy or UCB1?
goalChecks.expects: Arms: the 4 headlines; reward: click (1) or no click (0); rounds: visitors. Check: click rates roughly stable over time, showing a headline doesn't change later visitors, many visitors compared with 4 arms. Then UCB1, because exploration fades and regret stays lower over many rounds; watch for drift in click rates.

exam.question: Arm A has mean 0.9 and arm B has mean 0.6. Over 200 rounds a strategy pulls A 150 times and B 50 times. What is its regret, and what would greedy's regret be if it locked onto B from the start?
exam.reference: 50 × 0.3 = 15; locked onto B for all 200 rounds: 200 × 0.3 = 60.

exam.question: Why does UCB1 end up with lower regret than ε-greedy with ε = 0.1 over a million rounds?
exam.reference: ε-greedy keeps picking at random on 10% of rounds forever, so its regret grows linearly. UCB1's bonus shrinks as arms are tried, so it explores less and less and its regret grows only logarithmically.

exam.question: A streaming service shows each user one of 5 thumbnails for a film and wants as many clicks as possible. Describe it as a bandit and choose a strategy.
exam.reference: Arms: thumbnails; reward: click or not; rounds: users. Assumptions to check: click rates stable over time, one user's thumbnail doesn't change the next user's behaviour, many users compared with 5 arms. UCB1, because exploration fades and long-run regret is lower.
